ui.cover_lede: A textbook of the C++ programming language for Visual Studio Code, from your first program to classes, templates and the standard library. Every lesson has a working example in isiZulu, isiXhosa, siSwati, isiNdebele, Sesotho, Setswana, Sepedi, Xitsonga, Tshivenḓa and Afrikaans.
ui.fact1: From your first program to classes, templates, files and the standard library.
ui.fact2: Each example was compiled and run in all ten languages and printed exactly the same as the C++.
ui.fact3: Install the Soga extension in VS Code, save your file as name.zu.soga (or your language) and press Run.
ui.start1: In VS Code open Extensions, search Soga and click Install. You also need a C++ compiler: g++ on Windows and Linux, clang++ on macOS.
ui.start2: Save your program with your language in its name, for example {h}.
ui.start3: Press Run (▷, top right). The output appears in the terminal, and any errors are shown in your language.
ui.stdin_title: What was typed while it ran
ui.serial_note: Recorded by compiling and running this example. All ten language versions printed exactly the same.
ui.copy_note: Copy the example into a new file in VS Code, save it with your language in the name and press Run. The C++ tab shows the same program in standard C++.
ui.words_desc: Every C++ keyword and standard-library word Soga knows. Click a word that has a lesson to open it. Names you choose yourself are written the same in every language.
ui.foot1: Soga C++ Textbook · written by Mzwandile Zulu · Creative Minds Technologies
ui.foot3: Explanations are in English for now; the words and every example are in all ten languages. The words are a first draft that native speakers are reviewing.

entries.title: Soga in VS Code
entries.desc: Install the Soga extension in Visual Studio Code (search "Soga" under Extensions) and a C++ compiler (g++ on Linux and Windows, clang++ on macOS). Save your program with your language in the file name, for example hello.zu.soga for isiZulu or hello.ve.soga for Tshivenda. Press Run (the triangle at the top right) and the output appears in the terminal. Errors are shown in your language, and hovering over a word shows what it means in C++.

entries.title: The main function
entries.desc: Every program starts at main(). The code between { and } runs from top to bottom. return 0 at the end tells the computer that the program finished without problems.

entries.title: #include and using namespace
entries.desc: #include brings in a library: iostream for input and output, string for text, vector for lists, and so on. The names in the standard library live in the namespace std; "using namespace std;" lets you write cout instead of std::cout.

entries.title: Output: cout and endl
entries.desc: cout writes to the screen. Join several values with <<. endl, or "\n" inside the text, starts a new line.

entries.title: Comments
entries.desc: Comments are notes for people. The compiler ignores them. Write them in any language you like; Soga never translates or changes them.

entries.title: Variables
entries.desc: A variable is a named box that holds a value. Give it a type, a name and a value. You can change the value later.

entries.title: const
entries.desc: const makes a value that can never change. The compiler stops you if you try.

entries.title: Input: cin
entries.desc: cin reads what the user types. >> puts the typed value into a variable. It reads one word or one number at a time.
entries.output:
Name? Age? 
Thandi will be 16 next year.

entries.title: Data types
entries.desc: int holds whole numbers, long larger whole numbers, float and double numbers with a decimal point (double is more precise), char one character, and bool true or false. unsigned means "no negative numbers".

entries.title: sizeof
entries.desc: sizeof tells you how many bytes a type or a variable uses in memory.

entries.title: auto
entries.desc: auto lets the compiler choose the type from the value.

entries.title: Type conversion
entries.desc: Change a value from one type to another. Dividing two whole numbers drops the fraction; convert one to double first to keep it.

entries.title: Arithmetic operators
entries.desc: Add, subtract, multiply, divide and % (the remainder after dividing). ++ adds one and -- takes one away.

entries.title: Assignment operators
entries.desc: x += 3 is a short way of writing x = x + 3. The same works for -, *, / and %.

entries.title: Comparison operators
entries.desc: Compare two values. The answer is true (printed as 1) or false (printed as 0).

entries.title: Logical operators
entries.desc: Combine true/false values. You can write the words, or the symbols && (and), || (or) and ! (not); both mean the same.

entries.title: Strings
entries.desc: A string holds text. Join strings with +. Include <string> to use them.

entries.title: length, size and access
entries.desc: length() and size() give the number of characters. s[0] or s.at(0) gives the first character; at() also checks that the position exists.

entries.title: append and insert
entries.desc: append() adds text at the end; insert() puts text in at a position.

entries.title: substr, find and replace
entries.desc: substr() cuts out part of a string. find() gives the position of some text (or string::npos if it is not there). replace() swaps part of the string for new text.

entries.title: getline
entries.desc: cin stops at the first space. getline() reads the whole line, spaces included.

entries.title: to_string and stoi
entries.desc: to_string() turns a number into text; stoi() and stod() turn text into a whole number or a decimal number.

entries.title: Comparing strings
entries.desc: == checks whether two strings are the same. compare() gives 0 when equal, less than 0 or more than 0 for alphabetical order. empty() is true for a string with no characters.

entries.title: Characters: toupper, isdigit
entries.desc: Check or change one character: is it a digit, a letter, a space? Make it a capital or a small letter.

entries.title: max, min, abs
entries.desc: The larger of two values, the smaller of two values, and a number without its minus sign.

entries.title: sqrt, pow, round
entries.desc: Square roots, powers, and rounding to the nearest whole number, down (floor) or up (ceil). Include <cmath>.

entries.title: sin, cos, hypot
entries.desc: Trigonometry with angles in radians, and hypot() for the long side of a right-angled triangle.

entries.title: Formatting numbers
entries.desc: fixed with setprecision(n) shows exactly n decimals, which is right for money. setw(n) pads a value to n characters to make columns. Include <iomanip>.

entries.title: if, else if, else
entries.desc: Run code only when a condition is true. else if tests another condition; else runs when none of them was true.

entries.title: Short if: ? :
entries.desc: A one-line if that chooses between two values.

entries.title: switch, case, default
entries.desc: Choose one of many paths by the value of a number or character. End each case with break; default runs when no case matches.

entries.title: while
entries.desc: Repeat a block for as long as a condition stays true.

entries.title: do ... while
entries.desc: Like while, but the block always runs at least once, because the test is at the end.

entries.title: for
entries.desc: Repeat a block a set number of times: start, keep going while the condition is true, and take a step each time.

entries.title: Nested loops
entries.desc: A loop inside a loop. The inner loop runs completely for each round of the outer loop, which is how you make tables.

entries.title: for-each loop
entries.desc: Go through every item in an array, vector or string, without counting positions yourself.

entries.title: break and continue
entries.desc: break leaves the loop straight away. continue skips the rest of this round and goes on with the next one.

entries.title: Arrays
entries.desc: An array holds a fixed number of values of the same type, numbered from 0.

entries.title: Array size
entries.desc: sizeof of an array is its size in bytes. Divide by the size of one item to get the number of items.

entries.title: Two-dimensional arrays
entries.desc: An array of arrays: rows and columns, like a table or a game board.

entries.title: std::array
entries.desc: A fixed-size array that knows its own size() and works with the standard algorithms.

entries.title: struct
entries.desc: Group several related values into one new type.

entries.title: enum and enum class
entries.desc: A list of named choices. enum class keeps the names inside the type (Color::Red), which avoids mix-ups.

entries.title: Type names: using and typedef
entries.desc: Give an existing type a new, clearer name.

entries.title: References
entries.desc: A reference is another name for the same variable. Changing the reference changes the original.

entries.title: Pointers
entries.desc: A pointer holds the address of a variable. &x gives the address; *p reaches the value it points to. nullptr means it points to nothing.

entries.title: new and delete
entries.desc: new makes a value in memory that lives until you delete it. Every new needs a delete; smart pointers (below) do this for you.

entries.title: Functions
entries.desc: A function is a named block of code that you can call again and again. void means it gives nothing back; otherwise return sends a value back.

entries.title: Default parameters
entries.desc: A parameter can have a value that is used when the caller leaves it out.

entries.title: Pass by reference
entries.desc: With & the function works on the caller's own variable, so it can change it. Without & it gets a copy.

entries.title: Overloading
entries.desc: Several functions may share a name if their parameters differ. C++ picks the right one.

entries.title: Recursion
entries.desc: A function that calls itself, each time with a smaller problem, until it reaches a simple case.

entries.title: Lambdas
entries.desc: A small function without a name, written where you need it. Lambdas are often given to sort() and other algorithms.

entries.title: Classes and objects
entries.desc: A class describes a kind of thing: what it knows (member variables) and what it can do (methods). An object is one thing made from that class.

entries.title: Constructors and destructors
entries.desc: A constructor runs when an object is made and sets it up. A destructor (~Name) runs when the object is finished.

entries.title: public, private, getters and setters
entries.desc: private members can only be used inside the class; public ones from anywhere. Keep data private and give public functions to read and change it safely (encapsulation).

entries.title: this
entries.desc: Inside a method, this points to the object itself. It helps when a parameter has the same name as a member.

entries.title: static members
entries.desc: A static member belongs to the class, not to one object, so all objects share it.

entries.title: Inheritance and protected
entries.desc: A class can inherit everything from another class and add its own parts. protected members can be used by child classes but not from outside.

entries.title: virtual and override
entries.desc: With virtual, a child class can replace a method, and the right version runs even when you hold the object as its parent type (polymorphism).

entries.title: Abstract classes
entries.desc: A method written = 0 has no body; every child class must provide one. A class with such a method is abstract: you cannot make objects of it directly.

entries.title: Operator overloading
entries.desc: Teach +, ==, << and other operators what to do with your own classes.

entries.title: friend
entries.desc: A friend function may use the private members of a class.

entries.title: try, catch, throw
entries.desc: throw signals that something went wrong; try marks code that might fail; catch handles the problem so the program can continue.

entries.title: runtime_error and what()
entries.desc: The standard error types carry a message, which what() returns. at() throws out_of_range when a position does not exist.

entries.title: Writing and reading files
entries.desc: ofstream writes to a file and ifstream reads from it, using << and getline just like cout and cin. Include <fstream>.

entries.title: stringstream
entries.desc: A stringstream lets you read from or write to a string as if it were a file, which is handy for splitting text into numbers.

entries.title: vector
entries.desc: A list that can grow and shrink. push_back() adds at the end; size() counts the items; [] or at() reads one.

entries.title: vector: front, back, pop_back, erase, clear
entries.desc: Read the first and last items, remove the last one, insert or erase at a position, or empty the whole list.

entries.title: list
entries.desc: A linked list: quick to add and remove items at the front, at the back and in the middle.

entries.title: stack
entries.desc: Last in, first out, like a pile of plates: push() puts on top, top() looks at the top, pop() takes it off.

entries.title: queue
entries.desc: First in, first out, like a taxi rank: push() joins at the back, front() is the next one, pop() lets it go.

entries.title: deque
entries.desc: A double-ended queue: add and remove at both ends quickly.

entries.title: set
entries.desc: A collection of unique values, kept in order. Adding a value twice keeps only one; count() tells you whether a value is there.

entries.title: map
entries.desc: Pairs of keys and values, sorted by key, like a dictionary or a price list. Use m[key] to set or read; find() checks whether a key exists.
entries.output:
bread: R18
eggs: R42
milk: R25
no tea

entries.title: unordered_map
entries.desc: Like map, but not sorted, and usually faster for looking things up.

entries.title: pair and tuple
entries.desc: A pair holds two values (first and second); a tuple holds any number, read with get<position>.

entries.title: sort and reverse
entries.desc: sort() puts items in order (smallest first, or in any order you choose with a lambda); reverse() turns the order around. Include <algorithm>.

entries.title: find, count, max_element
entries.desc: Search a collection: find() finds a value, count() counts how often it appears, max_element() and min_element() find the biggest and smallest.

entries.title: accumulate and iota
entries.desc: accumulate() adds up everything in a collection; iota() fills it with 1, 2, 3, ... Include <numeric>.

entries.title: binary_search and unique
entries.desc: binary_search() quickly checks a sorted collection for a value. unique() with erase() removes repeated neighbours.

entries.title: Iterators
entries.desc: An iterator points at one item of a collection. begin() is the first item and end() is just past the last. *it reads the item.

entries.title: unique_ptr and make_unique
entries.desc: A smart pointer that owns its object and deletes it automatically when it is no longer used, so you never forget delete.

entries.title: shared_ptr and make_shared
entries.desc: A smart pointer that several owners can share. The object is deleted when the last owner is gone.

entries.title: Your own namespace
entries.desc: Put your own names in a namespace so they cannot clash with names from libraries.

entries.title: constexpr and static_assert
entries.desc: constexpr values are worked out while compiling. static_assert checks a rule while compiling and stops the build if it is broken.

entries.title: optional
entries.desc: An optional either holds a value or holds nothing, which is clearer than using a special number such as -1.

entries.title: numeric_limits
entries.desc: The largest and smallest values a type can hold.

entries.title: Random numbers: rand and srand
entries.desc: rand() gives a pseudo-random number; srand() sets the starting point. The same seed always gives the same numbers, which is useful for testing; use srand(time(0)) for different numbers each run.
